V Rising honestly is one of the best survival experiences out there, in my opinion. It kind of builds on the usual foundations you already know from the genre but it also has this strong identity, the atmosphere, and a very clear dedication to the vampire fantasy so it never really feels like yet another copy, in a sea of overcrowded releases. In a genre where a lot of titles blend together, V Rising kind of slips through and finds its own spot, and it does it in a way that leaves a mark, for real.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Atmosphere & Identity[/h2]

What really, like instantly drew me into V Rising was the atmosphere. The game kind of fully commits to its gothic vampire vibe, building a world that feels elegant, dark, and honestly pretty immersive. Even the way the architecture sits, the environments look, and how the enemies are designed, it all adds up. Like, every little part helps the fantasy of being a rising vampire lord, not just another survivor wandering through some harsh world. Every region, every castle, even the enemies they all stack up into that fantasy of becoming a rising vampire lord, not merely another survivor running around, grabbing resources in some hostile place. And more, it really seems to understand who it is. A lot of survival games talk about freedom, but then they end up making you feel kinda aimless, like ok…now what?. V Rising goes another route, because it keeps throwing you a clear sense of purpose and steady progression, almost all the time.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Progression & Systems[/h2]

The progression system is honestly one of the stronger parts, like it really keeps pulling you forward. Each boss isn’t just… you know, another obstacle on the way. when you beat them you get worthwhile rewards that expand what you can do right away, and also push you into new directions. So it feels like this steady loop where every win matters, every little advance feels earned, not like it was handed to you. More importantly, most players almost always know what they’re supposed to do next and how to get there. So instead of spending all day digging through guides, and wikis, you can actually spend your time playing the game.
Also, the boss lineup is a great. They each bring their own vibe themes, mechanics, and combat rhythm, so progression doesn’t turn into the same routine over and over. The game keeps dropping fresh kinds of trouble, which means the whole experience stays interesting from beginning till the end, even when you think you’ve seen it all. And beyond fighting, the systems for prisoners and servants really add to the vampire fantasy. It’s not only about surviving anymore. You’re building influence, organizing power, and setting control over what’s happening around you. That makes you feel like an actual vampire ruler, which is basically exactly the goal the game is aiming for. Then there’s the building system, which honestly deserves credit too. Sure, it’s simpler than a lot of other survival games, but that simplicity works in its favor. It’s smooth to use, efficient, and it doesn’t usually turn into some annoying grind of frustration. 
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Boss Design & Endgame Frustrations[/h2]

That said, the game is not without a few flaws, it kind of shows. Some of the endgame bosses felt frustrating though, not really because they were straight up difficult. It was more that a number of these encounters seem to lean on mechanics, and odd little gimmicks that occasionally feel kind of disconnected from the boss overall design. Instead of actually testing mastery of the game combat systems, those moments sometimes manufacture frustration for reasons that feel… sort of artificial. Not the nice kind of challenge, the kind that you can’t quite tie back to anything. A tough boss can be incredibly satisfying, no question. But a frustrating boss leaves, a totally different, impression in your head.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]The Endgame Grind[/h2]

My biggest criticism, however, kinda lies with the endgame grind. I get that resource gathering is a basic part of the survival genre , and I dont really mind grinding when it feels meaningful. The issue is that a lot of the endgame asks players to keep repeatedly gathering resources they have already farmed like a hundred times throughout the whole game . At that point it stops feeling like real progression and starts feeling more like a chore , you know? What used to be engaging slowly turns into something repetitive, and then the pacing kinda suffers because of it.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Music[/h2]

One small thing I kinda wish the game had done differently is how it handles major boss themes. The soundtrack is fine, but honestly I would have loved unique musical themes for the most important encounters, like not just the same overall vibe. At the very least, the final boss of each act could have had its own signature track. Memorable music has this weird way to elevate the fights and stick in your head long after the battle ends. A special theme for those key moments could have made several of the great bosses feel truly unforgettable, like Simon Belmont, for example.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Despite a few frustrations with some boss mechanics, and the sheer amount of grinding that keeps popping up in the later parts of the game, V Rising stays a pretty exceptional experience.  
The whole atmosphere is captivating, the progression feels consistently rewarding, and the systems somehow just fit together like they belong there, to deliver one of the best survival experince out there. Very few survival games manage to balance approachability, real depth, and a clear identity, and as far as I can tell V Rising does.
9.5/10

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Judging by first 30-ish hours this game would be almost a 10/10.

Endgame it can become an unrewarding slog and some bosses are an insane difficulty spike.

I still recommend it.

[h1]Description[/h1]
It's a semi-survival build/craft/combat game.

You play as a vampire and your goal is to increase your powers through crafting, killing bosses and building a sick castle.

You can select 3 spells from a pretty large assortment of different schools of magic + you get up to 2 skills attached to your weapon type. All skills and spells are cooldowns, there is no mana here. You can dodge and hit things with a basic attack. Low HP enemies can be drained of blood.

Draining enemies of blood will turn your class into that of the target. Each class has it's own passive bonuses and quality. For example a Rogue with 50% blood quality will give you about half of available stat bonuses of the Rogue class. Your blood depletes passively and more through automatic or active healing, so from time to time you need to snack. This will always change your class and blood quality, so hunting for tasty targets can be rewarding.

You can craft basic equipment through a menu. For more advanced stuff you need to build a castle and some crafting facilities first.

Castle has a core that you can plop down at any of unclaimed territories. Then you build castle around the core. You start off without being able to build actual castle walls, but you can place some wooden palisades. Unlocking new craft/build options is mostly done through killing bosses.

These bosses are unique enemies, usually present in special areas withing the game. You can track them through a menu, which will give you a trail to follow. Bosses have special attacks that you may need to learn how to deal with to fight them efficiently.

Materials for building/crafting are obtained by mining/logging or from enemy NPC camps. Each camp has different resources that are common in it. Mines may be filled with copper, while graveyards are good source of bone. You can also trade for some items with merchants if you find money for it.

As you advance through the crafting tree you will gain access to more and more bosses and more and more upgrades.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ Neat presentation[/b]
Graphics are clean and readable while containing enough detail to be interesting.

[b]+ Variety[/b]
There is a good variety of different spell schools, each one with it's own gimmick. Blood school lets you life leech on spell hits, while undead school lets you summon skeletons for example. Coupled with decent weapon variety and 2 skills for each of those weapon types as well as equipment modifiers there's enough stuff to try for anybody to find something that works for their playstyle.

[b]+ Combat[/b]
It's quick without feeling spammy. Different bosses encourage different playstyles or spell/weapon combos. Your dodge move has 8 second cooldown so you can't always rely on that to get you out of way of big moves and some enemies can hurt you a lot if you have no way to mitigate. Spells that provide shielding or counter-skills are helpful in those situations, but you can also just keep your distance and spam projectiles if you build around it.

[b]+ Bosses[/b]
While most early bosses are pretty boring and generic, that changes quickly. Some bosses are really fun to fight and all of them reward you with new crafting/building plans so it's always exciting to fight them. There's enough variety in boss design too - you get your badass beasts or monsters as well as elite bandit lords or crusaders or even vampire hunters. It can get crazy when your fight gets interrupted by a fking Simon Belmont (yes, he is in this game). I also like their audio design as most of them speak, taunting you at the start of the fight, etc.

Unfortunately there are also some very bad bosses too.

[b]+ Castle management[/b]
It's fun to build up your base and upgrade stuff. Later on you can also convert enemies to your cause by making them vampire thralls or put some in cells to act as your blood source. There's enough variety of clutter items to make your castle cozy.

[b]+ Progression[/b]
Between crafting, building, boss hunting and material farming there's always something to do and you will always have at least 1 clear goal in order to advance in the tech tree. For example you may find armor plans that require cotton, but you can't grow it yourself, so you can invade one of the NPC cotton farms and take it.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- Travel[/b]
By default you cannot teleport using unlockable waypoints if you have any resources. Later on you will get access to some other forms of transportation, but travel times can still be very tedious.

Suffice to say that I ended up modifying my default game settings to allow myself to teleport with resources.

Worst thing is charming enemies and having them follow you to your castle as you cannot switch to a different form if you have someone charmed. Have fun walking several kilometers home while avoiding enemies so that your follower doesn't get squished. It's especially painful when you happen to find a 100% blood quality enemy and just want to get him home, but some bomb-throwing a-hole decides to blow everything up, including his charmed buddy.

[b]- Bad bosses[/b]
Several starter bosses are unremarkable, but that's ok.

Pre-ultimate boss is unreasonably difficult even compared to the last one. I had to lower the difficulty because learning to beat him on normal would probably take me another 4-5h and by that time I was done with the game and just wanted to see the end.

Losing to bosses drains your blood and lets you respawn at any teleport, meaning you will have to walk back to boss arena to retry. It also depletes some of your gear's durability and repairing endgame gear takes a ton of rare resources that you may have to spend hours on obtaining.

This makes those bosses not exciting to learn like in souls games, but actually discouraging and needlessly punishing. One should not be forced to grind for hours just to keep trying at a boss, this is insane.

There are 2 bosses in this game that I would categorize as unreasonable, I was able to beat 1 of them on normal through persistence, but the pre-ultimate one broke me.

[b]- Some resources hard to get[/b]
Parts can be tricky to obtain because they only appear in specific enemy camps as resource you can mine. Grease is similar, but at least you can use some grease and mid-tier materials to generate more grease. Pristine and Bat leather drops in specific zones and you will have to commit significant amount of time to farm for them.

Gold can also be a pain, because only one type of enemies drop resources for it, unlike other metals which can be obtained in plenty amounts from mines.

[b]- Lots of farming[/b]
Especially near the end of the game. Endgame gear will not only cost rarer resources, but also more of them than early game stuff.

Amount of farming is fine in first 3 acts, but act 4 and endgame becomes unreasonable.

[b]- Ending[/b]
Beating last boss doesn't really end in any interesting event or anything which was disappointing.

[h1]Lowdown[/h1]
It's probably in top 5 games I played this year. Honestly when I play something for this long and I STILL want more when it ends - this has to mean the game is good. I enjoyed almost every mechanic this game has and when I was done this game has left a hole similar to when I finished Subnautica. Even comparing this game to the masterpiece that first Subnautica is means that it's a worthwhile purchase, even full-price.

V Rising at the first glance looks pretty much a typical isometric action-RPG, like Path of Exile, Van Helsing, Grim Dawn, and many more. However, there is a catch and a twist, turning everything upside down. 

You're playing for an ever-bloodthirsty and power hungry, monster vampire, who, at least in theory, dominates over all other lifeforms, slaying, bending, robbing and reshaping this given world as it pleases.

The game is rogue-like, to the point that mobs are resurrecting faster than you clear the given locations. Meaning, you can get in the loop in some scenarios, forced to kill or run from the very same bosses that you've already downed 5 minutes ago. 

Also, and that's a major issue actually, the game is server-action type. Thus, even if you want to play it solo, you can't pause the process, and also, that all your main progress stored not in the local save file, but on the server, which will turn it all down eventually. So, if you are, like me, not a regular player, and can spend time to games maybe on the monthly basis, be prepared to the problem that you'll need to start it over and over again.

Finally, with all those dozens of different bosses, all that variety of biomes and regular hazards, the main theme of the game is not about fighting. It's about grinding more and more resources, to build and enhance your base and equipment, to be able [b][url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oSPT27XyY1U]to do more killing, looting and crafting[/url][/b]... Et cetera.

Now, when we're done with naming things that can be relatively called the downsides, let's say why it's a great game. The first thing coming to my mind is about seamlessness of all things involved. 

Different locations, biomes, all are tightly wrapped together, and you can travel between them almost freely... If you're powerful enough to run through the patrolling mobs. And with that, the game constantly creates intermedia between those different world parts, some presumably generic episodes of different mobs travelling just like you in this world, and starting some local mayhems here and there... Okay, one story, to provide you a typical experience.

Once upon a time, I was shuffling in the central region, and crossed paths with the dangerous vampire hunter, a real tough nut case, with a powerful stunning, distance controlling and AOE attacks. I was not able to kill him fast, or run away, so, our struggle kinda burned out a massive piece of land, along with all light mobs usually walking around. And then, a stranger comes by the road, and takes a hit from some AOE attack. Turns out, it is one more travelling boss, who's hostile both to me AND vampire hunter, so, [b][url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PgAKzmWmuk]a Mexican three-way duel[/url][/b] starts now. Apparently, that third guy was weaker, so he felt first. But, since there's a special effect for consuming every boss, a life restoring power ups, and a powerful blast, once I've finished that second boss, the blast took out the vampire hunter, who could last much longer any other way... Just a one, almost regular, near to generic situation...

Your base, your castle, that emphasizes yours progress, adding more and more new mechanics, possibilities, and interrelations between your actions and abilities, is really fun to build. You're starting with the main idea to have a roof above your head, which quickly evolves into the factory-type constellation of rooms and mechanisms, that recycles, refines and build anew more and more complicated power enhancers and aesthetic improvements... 

You can spend dozens of hours in that game, not fighting enemies or grinding materials, but purely modelling and reformatting your castle. And maybe even your appearance, if you need it.

V Rising provides a proper gameplay experience for all the adorers of vampires aesthetic, and also, many fun and challenging battles with tough enemies, and hundreds of ways to remade your castle, any way you like. All in all, it's a great indie title, respectful to his players, and providing a somewhat unique, by the combination of different patterns, gameplay, which I liked, after trying it in that free weekend event, which was certainly [b][url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VM2eLhvsSM]a good promotion idea[/url][/b]. Despite all my personal displease with the idea of playing villains. My mark is 8/10.

PS: You don't need DLCs to get a complete with achievements, which is also a point to like and recommend the game. Can't say that DLCs are worthless, if you're a fan, but, yeah, you'll be good without them.

This game mainly utilizes a Castle system, in which all your processing, refinement and other such machines can be placed and utilized. There's a lot of different types of systems in this game to learn, and almost all the youtube videos about some of them suck (looking at you servant system). Good things:

-Bosses were fun and required strategy. I found myself switching spells and trying different ideas a lot to take down certain challenges. -Base Building and Crafting was well thought out for a lot of it, and didn't appear to have any issues or confusion. If you love building your own custom castles, this is the game to do it.

Bad things:
-Farming materials. In a group of 3, farming materials was a constant issue. This was obviously expected (this is a open world survival craft for crying out loud) but there was some things in particular that definitely stood out to us as being... excessive. 
For example, gold ingots. To get your best neck piece, you need 6 of them, which is made with 8 jewelry per. V Rising is an exceedingly solid experience, especially with a little tweaking of the settings. The game consists of a relatively standard progression system through a pre-designed world with several biomes with a small degree of randomization to keep things a little fresh.  You move upwards through various tool and armor tiers by variously harvesting, chopping, mining, looting, and killing things in the world around you, bringing your spoils to your castle. 

There is a day/night cycle, but as this is a game about vampires, the "safe" period is the night, and the "unsafe" period is the day. This wouldn't be terribly interesting by itself other the novelty, but, critically, it is still possible to go outside during the day by literally sticking to the shadows - manuevering from the shadow of a tree, to a wall, to a boulder, to inside a hut or house, and so on, which makes the decisionmaking about when you decide to go out raiding or harvesting a little more nuanced.

The basebuilding admirably refuses to get bogged down in the tedious lists of components like "Platform 1x2" and "Inverted Corner Stair 2x2"s that afflict other games, opting instead for an initially simple set of castle components. Additionally, your castle can only be built in certain "plots". There a good ~140 or so castle plots throughout the map, and these aren't separate instances; they are part of the map itself as traversable land and contain resources to harvest when not in use (and almost all of them won't be in use because you can have up to 5 castles) and take a variety of shapes and sizes, which will act to govern how your castle layout ends up forming. While there can be an initial reaction of dislike to the size limits, I very quickly began to appreciate how it prevented me from just creating the vampire equivalent of the Minecraft dirt block house. If you want a good castle, you (usually) can't just build a big cube filled with all your stuff, especially because you are rewarded for having distinct rooms for e.g. forging, workshopping, imprisoning captives, etc. You are also gradually given many cosmetics to make your castle look aesthetically pleasing and detailed, but even within the first ~5 hours or so, you can make a base that looks pretty snazzy.

The combat in this game is, I think, its weakest aspect, but it isn't "bad" by any means. You can make a selection of weapons - e.g. a sword, axes, a mace, a spear, etc - and you unlock more options as your progress through the game, such as bows, crossbows, daggers, and whips, to name but a few. There is also a selection of six overarching spell schools (Blood, Chaos, Frost, Storm, Illusion, Unholy) in which you can more-or-less freely switch between spells you unlock through the game depending on the situation you find yourself in. Most builds will opt for a combination of spells and weapons. This is the great part of the combat system - there's a good array of possible builds and weapon-spell combinations. 

Where the combat begins to flag a little is when this is actually brought in the vicinity of enemies. The balancing of enemy stats against your own is fairly lopsided in favor of the enemy unless you outlevel them, resulting in most on-level encounters being quite close. A large part of the reason why this occurs is twofold: healing in combat is difficult to impossible, and your dodges are on a longish (~6-8 second) cooldown. This combination means that it's hard to ever feel like you're outskilling and outplaying enemies through great dodging and taking the correct moments to heal, and instead can often feel like you're just seeing whether or not "my effective health - enemy damage" is a positive number over the course of an encounter. This dynamic is only further amplified in bossfights, which are otherwise usually fun and creative encounters. I say "usually" because there are some real stinkers out there, especially towards lategame, where getting repeatedly stunned/frozen/incapacitated without being able to do much about it, as well as drowned in bullethells and summoned enemy hordes becomes more common than not. 

I found that in a majority of boss fights, I would begin with a bold melee strategy, my healthbar would rapidly deteriorate because the bosses attack more frequently than you can dodge making it mathematically impossible to avoid taking damage at close range (and the dodges also seem to have minimal i-frames and perhaps none at all). I would then be forced to switch to a much more boring and time-consuming ranged strategy where I just ran away all the time and spammed spells and bowshots at long range - repeat until the boss dies. Certain bosses can be found roaming the roads, which presents an additional problem as you not only get mostly killed by the mobs surrounding them before you can even attack the boss, but being forced to resort to the aforementioned ranged strategy means that them losing aggro and rapidly regenerating their health becomes a serious and annoying problem. So in all, while the bosses were usually engaging and creative, they are also the single worst part of the game, and I frequently found myself actively procrastinating moving onwards in progression because I was loathing what this next round of boss fights might have in store for me.

The only other major factor to note is the resource gathering systems. I found this pretty good, with perhaps its greatest sin being its inability to break free of the relative tedium that so many other games in its genre suffer from. To V Rising's credit, the proportion of resources you gain and can carry can be adjusted in settings (so you can still plenty enjoy this game if you happen to have one of those "job" things I've heard so much about), as can other options like whether some resources cannot be teleported. Not being able to teleport certain resources strongly encourages you to actually engage in non-teleport transportation methods like horses, which I think is *generally* fine, but traversing half the map back to your castle after a resource collection run does get pretty monotonous after a while, and I think the game could perhaps offer better scaling to traversal speeds or alternative methods for the lategame. The speed at which resources craft also leaves a lot to be desired, but it does at least prompt you to make bigger castles with more machines running in parallel, so I understand the idea there. You can also create "servants" which effectively gather resources for you over time, and I recommend fully engaging with this system as it cuts down on a considerable amount of the grinding time.

I have no complaints about the music or graphics. Neither of them absolutely blew me away, but both are appropriately stylized and of a consistently great quality. I also have nothing to say about the PvP aspects of the game, as I didn't engage with them (I have played in both pure coop and solo), but I can at least say that I never felt like I was playing an inferior product for not playing on a server, which is always nice for a game's longevity once updates inevitably cease and new games come out.

Its a fun game, but every major update requires starting a new game in order to experience the new content. If you like PvP then periodic resets might be just the thing to keep the game fresh and competitive. But if you want a PvE game where you can invest hundreds of hours building up a base, having to restart every update is just tedious.

Absolutely BRILLIANT. TL:DR:
If you like ARPGs, if you like MMO style boss fights, and you like crafting/base building, this game SHOULD be on your "Must Own" list.

(Quick note, I never engaged with the bigger online servers, or the PVP elements which seem to be a potentially large part of this game, I ONLY played it with friends on a private run server).

At almost every turn I found a mechanic where I went "Damn, any other dev would've made this painful and tedious" but these guys just never did, it truly felt like the game was made by gamers that have felt the pain of the Triple A industry's choices to "keep players playing more".

The Bosses:
Very VERY few of the bosses felt annoying, I'd say maybe 5-10% were annoying/bad, 20-40% were "filler bosses" (Somewhat simple mechanics, but could be deadly in their own right if you mess up), 15-20% were "spectacle bosses" (not too difficult, more about the theme or the experience) 20-30%  were ABSOLUTELY AMAZING fights, and then there was the last boss.. Truly felt like a final mythic raidboss in a WoW raid, some mechanics felt a liiiittle bs, but overall the fight was super good, and really hard. (Played through on the Normal Difficulty mode, and I plan to try Brutal at some point).

There are lore sections about each boss you're going out to hunt, if you wanna read them to immerse yourself even more in the world they are there, but you don't really need them if you're the type of player that just likes the mechanical/gameplay focused aspect.

The crafting/building system:
There are some parts that feel a little annoying or tedious here, but guess what, you can customize almost EVERY SINGLE MECHANIC IN THE GAME down to a minute degree.
Don't like durability burn? Turn it down by 25-50-75% or even clompletely off.
Don't like the mechanic that blockes you from using teleporters while carrying resources? Turn it off!
Want to reduce the amount of materials needed to craft because it feels too grindy? You can do it!
Want to reduce the amount of materials (or increase) you get from nodes so it becomes more (or less) grindy? Sure, why not!

One minor  gripe, when building you cannot turn off snapping, and sometimes even if you do a perfect run around your castle area with hedges or walls, something random from the environment will still block it or the like.
I found workarounds for most of it, but it's still a bit annoying and messed that experience up a little bit for me, at least until I found workarounds.

The world/Exploration:
Quest markers? That sounds lame! Go explore the world!
Need to find the next boss? Follow the trail! 
It's a simple work around to having a quest marker on your hud, but it makes the game so much more engaging, without making it tedious in any way.
The world zones are  varied and beautiful, you end up in some really cool locations, and the campaign will send you all over the map to find things you need, so slowly you'll explore everything as time goes.

Music/graphics:
The music is amazing, really great soundtrack, loved every second of it, super fitting.
Graphics, aside from the bit annoying "behind the character, arpg/mmo" style camera, the graphics themselves are pretty.

IMO, without a single doubt, one of the best ARPGs ever made.
I applaud these developers for several of the things they've done, absolutely puts most AAA Arpgs to shame!

So far i have spent 211 hours in the world Vardoran, and oh boy where do i even start..

For me, it captures the idea of an immortal vampire perfectly, from right after you awaken in the crypts, your nature is clear. You feast on mortals to savour the benefits of their blood, be it a worker to boost your gathering, a scholar to vastly empower your spellcasting, a brute to relish in the melee slaughter - you get the idea.

But, perhaps a boss ruins your day, or maybe the pesky sunlight leaves your great undead ruler-to-be a tad charred, in which case, get back to your grand castle. (Some of you might chose to just live with wooden walls, i suppose, to each their own.)

You could hunt for some good humans, scouring the streets for high end blood to bring back to your castle for your dark delights, be it imprisoning them in your own personal wineyard, or turning them into a vampire spawn/servant to roam your halls, guarding your castle or heading out on missions.

Not to mention the combat, which is the greatest i have had the pleasure to immerse myself in. Hunting powerful V-bloods to progress through the different tech stages, and unlocking powerful new spells that will allow you to greatly mix up your playstyle.

There is so much more that can be said about the game, so many fun things to do,  Yet i think i have said all that need to be said.

If you are still reading this review, give it a try. It is a fresh take on the survival setting, and it has completely consumed my free time. 

I cant wait for updates, if this is only the early access, the launched product is going to be a sight to behold.  If for some reason you do not feel it is worth the current cost, keep track of the game updates, the game is already a steal for the current cost.

Absolutely fantastic open-world (ish) survival game.  It's like if Ark: Survival Evolved and Diablo II had a vampiric baby.  

POSITIVES
* Combat is largely dependent on skill and not on RNG (very much a good thing in my opinion).  Meaty and satisfying.
* Building castles is great fun, as is sending minions on missions
* Your character feels powerful but not invincible - bosses are challenging but persistence and practice will get you through eventually.
*PVE - cooperative play is an absolute blast.  Share victory, share defeat, share that story of how your friend got absolutely mauled by a golem that one time...
* Vampires are just cool, alright.  I just think they're neat!

NEGATIVES
* Endgame content is somewhat lacking - once you've defeated the last of the V-Blood characters, there's really not much more to do as everything else feeds into levelling up in order to beat the next boss.  I'm assuming that this will be expanded on as the game proceeds through development, it's still in early access after all.
* PVP is not great.  Castles are forced to build "honeycomb" defences to slow down attackers which just result in every castle looking the same - a checkerboard of empty rooms.  Pretty boring.

OVERALL
I had a lot of fun with this title.  A LOT of fun.  But I'm not sure I'll play another SOLO run until some more content comes out.

Decent survival action game with a flavouring of RPG combat, although somewhat under-cooked in each aspects of its undertaking.

The game's presentation is great. Although the setting itself isn't unique, featuring very standard fantasy genre trope creatures, set pieces and designs. There isn't anything here that you haven't seen in other fantasy games, but this time you are playing as a vampire, so your castle exudes very Gothic styles and furniture. The graphics are nice, the lighting works well and night and day are remarkably different experiences visually. The only major dissonance here is really the use of low poly character models for the bosses and enemies, visually clashing with the detailed world assets.

There is a decent amount of foliage and clutter, and each biome feels distinct enough from one another to encourage exploration and provide diversity. Sound design is decent, although nothing too memorable.

Moving on to gameplay, the strengths and weaknesses are more pronounced. You play as a vampire with explicit goals of hunting down special bosses that award you new blueprints and powers on defeat. Similar to other genre staples, you can either use an altar at your castle to create a tracking trail that leads to the boss, or you can simply head to the area and find them as they are either always in an arena or have a set patrol route.

The bosses are varied enough to feel fun, although the first half of the bosses are simply just enhanced mobs, and the last few bosses are where it gets more interesting and challenging. There is a need to plan the time you engage these bosses, as the game's day night cycle means that in the day when the sun is out you can possibly be caught in an arena basked in sunlight, which casts a deadly ray on your vampire that can quickly finish you off.

The castle building is decent, and utilizes a gridbased expansion and construction system. This means that you can quickly build structures and alignment is easy, though it also means that the more avid builder might feel limited. There are a decent amount of crafting stations with your standard forge, woodwork, chemistry and sawmill, and a few other specific stations that involve blood refinement. Where the base building gets unique is the introduction of prison cells that allow you to lure charmed NPCs with a high blood quality back, imprisoning them and turning them into livestock. There are a number of farming stations available, although the steep material costs involved to even begin production of other materials can be off-putting. 

Crafting is one of the weakest points here, and while its generic tiered weapon crafting system is serviceable, the problem of the material acquisition rate rears its ugly head often. As an example, the mid game to late game crafting utilizes a lot of scourgestone in almost any high end crafting materials. Scourgestone is either found in graveyard areas, or crafted with a set of lesser materials that are still specific to find. Almost the entirety of your progression will be locked by scourgestone production rates, while other materials accumulate well into excess stacks. After the scourgestone drought ends, you will run into the next issue, scrolls, which are needed to randomly unlock a blueprint on your research desk, hoping for armor and weapon unlocks even as the RNG decides to unlock a furniture blueprint instead.

All these crafting woes lead to a massive grind for resources, one that can only countered by playing in larger coop parties or if PVP, raiding other castles. There needs to be more loot spots or more enemies and loot drops per spot for some materials, especially ones that bleed into multiple recipes.

The combat is quite engaging, it allows you to pick two spells, an ultimate and you have three weapon skills preset based on what weapon you are using. There are some neat combos here, and the telegraphing and real time evasion of attacks provide for a rather fun combat system that you can get better at with play. Much of the spell options are however, locked behind boss kills, and there is no other customisation which means that most players you encounter would be running similar builds that lack variety. You can select a class in essence by drinking blood from a creature or human of a particular class, and the quality of the blood determines how much buffs you receive. While interesting, it turns into a micromanagement game that can become annoying later on.

Loot is mostly restricted to more materials for crafting, and bosses do not drop unique gear outside of the one or two that do early game. Gear scales upwards with pure stats, so a higher level sword does nothing but increase your damage, and adds nothing else. This bland tiered gearing system can rear its ugly head later on when you begin to feel like there is a lack of motivation to earn new gear.

The game does have a lot of potential and is a blast to play with friends, but at the end of the day it feels like a lacking title that only slightly innovates from the standard genre tropes and then completely stops and doesn't take the game further. The systems work well together, but they do not work at the levels needed to make the game stand out. 

Early Access, keep an eye, decent for its price.

I have some major complaints about this game. It's a great experience in nearly all aspects across the board throughout first half of the game - really enjoyable, no matter if you're playing PVP or PVE. However, after playing the game for 20-30-something hours it becomes monotone and just... lazily designed. 


The entire game resolves around the simple paradygm of: 
- Kill X.
- Get recipe from killing X.
- Grind resources.
- Craft newly unlocked items, increase your gear level.
- You can now kill X2, rinse and repeat. 

And to noone's surprise - the whole cycle gets boring around 30 hours into the game. Especially since you can only come up with so many ideas for bosses, after that they just get annoying / repetetive. I swear to god, 80% of late game bosses revolve around shitty-area-denial-fuck-you-for-standing-there mechanics. Expect for the Old Wanderer, who's Micolash from Bloodborne incarnated - he causes psychological damage by making you chase him around an entire forest, filled with enemies while your vision is obscured to the point of not seeing your dick when you look down. Oh. And his health bar regenerates if you dare to stop for 5 seconds and he gets sufficiently far away.
 
And the fact that 95% of recipes for items / structures are randomized and you gotta hope for getting what you need / what you want doesn't help at all. Especially since this game gets really tough really quickly if you are undergeared. Which is also a sign of a bad game design - you are expected to follow a linear progression route, with nothing exciting ever happening. 

Another problem with this game for me was the terrible, terrible balancing for single player playthroughs. You are expected to play this game in co-op, with friends. If you want to play this game alone you're in for quite a challenging experience, since bosses will kick your ass if you are ever so slightly underleveled. Like, seriously. Devs came up with a fun servant system, where you can recruit enemies to serve you and venture on hunts, defend your castle etc. They couldn't add a function of using those servants to aid you in boss battles if playing solo? They could at least be a meat-shield or could pick you up when downed.

Overall it's a good game (and a great castle builder btw) with some annoying flaws.


@EDIT
Some people come here and call me out for accusing the game of getting boring after 20-30 hours of gameplay. My brothers in christ, I specified that boss hunting design gets boring. I've spent 90% of that playtime building castles. And so did / will you. The game requires you to kill repetitive bosses to progress the game without any chances of making a unique build - *this* gets boring, not the barbieland building aspect.
